name: Sateré-Mawé
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress; 3 further works by the same author (or citing it for stress) agree.

new_statements.quote: Como podemos observar nos dados apresentados acima, o acento recai sempre na sílaba final da palavra simples. [...] Podemos dizer que o acento é predizível, sempre incidindo na última sílaba da palavra simples, não sendo, portanto, distintivo na língua Sateré-Mawé. (p. 96) — Na junção de duas palavras simples para formar outra, o acento permanece fixo na última sílaba de cada palavra. Porém, o grau de intensidade da primeira palavra é mais fraco em relação à segunda, ou seja, o grau de emissão fonética é mais forte na última sílaba da palavra composta. (p. 97)
new_statements.translation: As we can observe in the data presented above, stress always falls on the final syllable of the simple word. [...] We can say that stress is predictable, always falling on the last syllable of the simple word, and is therefore not distinctive in the Sateré-Mawé language. (p. 96) — When two simple words are joined to form another, stress stays fixed on the last syllable of each word. However, the degree of intensity of the first word is weaker relative to the second, i.e. the phonetic prominence is strongest on the last syllable of the compound word. (p. 97)

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (final: final stress). Adds that stress is non-distinctive, that suffixed words re-stress on the new final syllable, that compounds keep a weaker final stress on each non-final member, and that vowel length in unstressed syllables does not attract stress. That dissertation, already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the last syllable of every simple word; it is predictable and non-contrastive. Suffixation keeps stress on the final syllable of the derived word (muse 'pepper' -> muse'ʔɨːp 'pepper tree'; wasa'ʔi 'açaí' -> wasaʔi'ʔip 'açaí palm'). In compounds each member keeps its final-syllable stress, with the last member's stress the strongest. Long vowels occur in unstressed syllables (saː'ri 'ant', suː'hu 'tobacco'), so weight does not attract stress; the metrical section (p. 99) treats them as non-head members of a right-headed foot. The chapter opens by noting that, as in Kamaiurá (Seki 2000:419), stress is predictable on the last syllable of the word (p. 95).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as such; in compounds the first member's final-syllable stress is kept but weaker than the last member's (p. 97), which amounts to a secondary stress on the final syllable of non-final compound members.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The author repeatedly flags the analysis as preliminary and not conclusive (p. 95: 'não chegamos a uma conclusão definitiva'; p. 104: 'O estudo do acento ainda não é conclusivo'), noting that sentence-level prosody and rhythmic typology remain to be studied.
new_statements.identity_note: The dissertation describes Sateré-Mawé as spoken in the Terra Indígena Andirá-Marau (Amazonas/Pará border), ~8,000 speakers, with no dialect distinguished; the work is a standard-variety description, not a dialect study.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the (now obtained) Silva 2005 phonology thesis at p.96, and two further primary works by the same fieldworker — a 2006 article devoted to Sateré-Mawé stress and the 2010 329-pp reference grammar (§3.5) — independently restate fixed, predictable, non-distinctive word-final stress on the phonological word, unchanged under suffixation and compounding. Franceschini 1999 is silent; no instrumental or later phonological study was found. Coding 'fixed final' (final stress) is therefore correct; keeping not in the strict set is defensible given Silva's own 'análise preliminar / não conclusivo' hedges, though no exceptions are reported. Record's grade field is empty and 'held' was empty: fill grade, register the three files, and correct the locator to ch.5 pp.95-105, quote p.96 (optionally add Silva 2010 §3.5 p.111 as a co-citation).
